Psychiatry · published research

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)

A 36-person sham-controlled trial reported lower HAMA anxiety scores after two weeks of 820-nm transcranial treatment and at follow-up. A separate small single-arm pilot also reported lower anxiety scores, but had no control group.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 36-person sham-controlled trial reported lower HAMA anxiety scores after two weeks of 820-nm transcranial treatment and at follow-up. A separate small single-arm pilot also reported lower anxiety scores, but had no control group.

Summary of the Evidence

The Brain > Anxiety mapping contains five titles: four human reports and one rat experiment. Only two human reports directly studied generalized anxiety disorder. The other clinical records concern persistent anxiety with depression or anxiety measured in a sleep and temporomandibular-disorder sample, so they are not direct GAD treatment trials.

Human and clinical evidence

Wang et al. randomized 36 people with GAD to active or sham transcranial near-infrared stimulation. The 820-nm treatment over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex was associated with lower Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale scores after two weeks and at follow-up (2023). Maiello et al.'s pilot recruited 15 adults, with 12 completing an eight-week single-arm treatment; anxiety scores fell from baseline, but without a control group the change cannot be attributed confidently to light (2019, DOI 10.1089/photob.2019.4677, Article). A later three-case series addressed persistent anxiety and depression during other treatment, while a small randomized study measured anxiety in people with sleep or jaw symptoms. Neither is a GAD cohort.

Animal evidence

One rat experiment measured anxiety-like behavior after transcranial PBM. It provides mechanistic context, not evidence that patients with GAD improve.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell, tissue, or ex-vivo study is listed for this indication.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The direct studies used transcranial near-infrared light. The randomized trial used 820 nm at the left prefrontal site; the pilot used an 830-nm LED headband for 20 minutes daily over eight weeks and reported 36 J/cm2 per session. Wavelength is the light's color band and influences how far it can pass through tissue. These small studies do not establish an optimal dose.

Interpretation

The randomized result supports a possible short-term score reduction for one transcranial protocol, but not remission or durable improvement. The uncontrolled pilot is supportive only as preliminary evidence. Independent trials should enroll diagnosed GAD populations and compare active light with credible sham treatment.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term anxiety-scale improvement after transcranial near-infrared treatment in one small randomized GAD trial Very low for remission, long-term benefit, or light treatment alone across GAD populations
Publications and records5 titles (narrow mapping to Brain > Anxiety; 2 human reports directly enrolled GAD)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One small sham-controlled trial directly enrolled people with GAD and reported lower anxiety scores. A separate pilot had no comparison group, while other records studied different anxiety populations. Replication in larger GAD samples with blinded ratings, functional outcomes, and follow-up is needed.
